en: Majjhima Nikāya 68:
The Discourse at Naḷakapāna.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans at Naḷakapāna in the Palāsa Grove.
Now at that time, several well-known clansmen who had gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness under the Blessed One were there:
the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Bhaddiya, the Venerable Kimbila, the Venerable Bhagu, the Venerable Koṇḍañña, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ānanda, and other well-known clansmen.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air surrounded by the community of monks.
Then the Blessed One, referring to those sons of good family, addressed the monks:
"Monks, as for those sons of good family who have out of faith gone forth from the home life into homelessness under me, are those monks, monks, delighted with the holy life?"
When this was said, those bhikkhus remained silent.
A second time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning those sons of good family:

"Bhikkhus, as for those sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, having dedicated themselves to me—do those bhikkhus, I ask you, delight in the holy life?"
A second time those bhikkhus remained silent.
A third time the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning those sons of good family:

"Bhikkhus, as for those sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, having dedicated themselves to me—do those bhikkhus, I ask you, delight in the holy life?"
A third time those bhikkhus remained silent.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"What if I were to question these sons of good family?"
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Anuruddhas, I hope you are delighted with the holy life?
“Truly, Bhante, we are delighted with the holy life.”
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!
This indeed, Anuruddhas, is worthy of you, sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith: that you should take delight in the holy life.
For you, Anuruddhas, are endowed with the excellence of youth, being in the prime of your age and possessing very black hair...”

You should enjoy sensual pleasures, Anuruddhas; for you have gone forth from the home life into homelessness while still endowed with the excellence of youth, in the first stage of life, with hair still very black.
Moreover, Anuruddhas, you have not gone forth from the home life into homelessness under compulsion by a king.

I have not gone forth from the home life into homelessness because I was led away by thieves, nor because I was oppressed by debt, nor because I was oppressed by fear, nor because I lacked a livelihood.
Rather, I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
“Is it not the case, Anuruddhas, that you have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘Perhaps an end might be made of this entire mass of suffering’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“And further, Anuruddha, what should be done by a clansman who has thus gone forth?
He should attain seclusion from sensual pleasures, seclusion from unwholesome states, and the joy and happiness [born of that seclusion], or something even more peaceful than that.
For if covetousness remains obsessing his mind, or ill will remains obsessing his mind...”
It persists by taking hold of the mind; sloth and torpor also persist by taking hold of the mind; restlessness and remorse also persist by taking hold of the mind;
doubt also persists by taking hold of the mind; discontent also persists by taking hold of the mind;
lethargy also persists by taking hold of the mind.

“Anuruddhas, one who does not attain seclusion from sensual pleasures, seclusion from unwholesome states, the joy and happiness [born of that seclusion], or anything more peaceful than that, does not have covetousness persistently take hold of his mind, nor does ill will...

take hold of his mind. “Anuruddhas, one who attains seclusion from sensual pleasures, seclusion from unwholesome states, the joy and happiness [born of that seclusion], or anything more peaceful than that, does not have covetousness persistently take hold of his mind, nor does ill will...”
Sloth and torpor do not persist by taking possession of the mind; restlessness and remorse do not persist by taking possession of the mind;
doubt does not persist by taking possession of the mind; discontent does not persist by taking possession of the mind;
and lethargy does not persist by taking possession of the mind.
“Anuruddhas, by seclusion from sensual pleasures and seclusion from unwholesome states, one attains rapture and happiness, or something even more peaceful than that.
What do you think, Anuruddhas:

do you have this thought regarding me—‘The tathāgata has not yet abandoned those taints that are subject to defilement, productive of renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death’?”
"Therefore, the Tathāgata, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, endures one thing; having reflected, avoids one thing; having reflected, dispels one thing.

"Venerable sir, it does not occur to us that 'those taints which are corrupting, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—these have not been abandoned by the Tathāgata.'"
"Therefore, the Tathāgata, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, endures one thing; having reflected, avoids one thing; having reflected, dispels one thing.
Thus, Bhante, we regard the Blessed One:

"Those taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and conducive to future birth, aging, and death—those have been abandoned by the Tathāgata."
"Therefore, the Tathāgata, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, he endures one thing; having reflected, he avoids one thing; having reflected, he dispels one thing.
"Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!

Those taints (āsava) of the Tathāgata—which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—have been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future."
"Just as, Anuruddha, a palmyra tree with its crown cut off is incapable of further growth,
even so, Anuruddha, whatever taints there are in the Tathāgata that lead to defilement, to renewed existence, to distress, to the ripening of suffering,
and to future birth, aging, and death— these have been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future."
Therefore, the Tathāgata, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, he endures one thing; having reflected, he avoids one thing; having reflected, he dispels one thing.
What do you think, Anuruddha, seeing what purpose does the Tathāgata declare the rebirths of disciples who have passed away?
“‘That one has been reborn there; that one has been reborn there’?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of these words. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”

“Anuruddha, it is not for the sake of deceiving people, nor for the sake of flattering people, nor for the sake of gain, honor, and renown, nor with the thought ‘let people know me thus,’ that the Tathāgata declares the rebirths of disciples who have passed away and died, saying:
‘So-and-so has been reborn there; so-and-so has been reborn there.
Yet, Anuruddha, there are sons of good family who possess faith, noble confidence, and noble gladness.”
Having heard that, they apply their minds toward that end.
For them, Anuruddha, this leads to welfare and happiness for a long time.
Here, Anuruddha, a bhikkhu hears:
‘A monk named so-and-so has passed away;
he was declared by the Blessed One to have been established in final knowledge.’
Furthermore, that venerable one has either seen for himself or heard by tradition concerning him:
"Such was the virtue of that venerable one; such was his Dhamma; such was his wisdom; such was his way of abiding; such was his liberation.
Recalling his faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, he directs his mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, a bhikkhu dwells in comfort.
Here, Anuruddha, a bhikkhu hears:
"A certain bhikkhu has passed away;..."
The Blessed One has declared of him:
‘With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to return from that world.
Furthermore, that venerable one has either been seen by him in person or heard of through tradition:
‘Such was the virtue of that venerable one,’ and ‘such was his Dhamma... such was his wisdom... such was his mode of dwelling...
such was his liberation, that venerable one,’ thinking thus, he directs his mind toward that goal by recollecting his faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
In this way too, Anuruddhas, a bhikkhu dwells in comfort.
In this case, Anuruddha, a bhikkhu hears:
"A bhikkhu named so-and-so has passed away;
he was declared by the Blessed One—"

‘With the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is a once-returner who, having come back to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering.
Furthermore, that venerable one has either been seen by him in person or heard of through tradition:
‘Such was the virtue of that venerable one; such was his Dhamma... such was his wisdom; such was his way of abiding; such was the liberation of that venerable one.’”
Thus, recollecting his faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, he directs his mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, a bhikkhu dwells in comfort.
Here, Anuruddha, a bhikkhu hears:
‘A bhikkhu named so-and-so has passed away;
he was declared by the Blessed One to be a stream-enterer,
no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment, through the complete destruction of three fetters.’
Furthermore, that venerable one has either seen for himself or heard by tradition:
“Such was the virtue of that venerable one; such was his Dhamma... such was his wisdom... such was his way of abiding... such was his liberation.
Recalling his faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, he directs his mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, a bhikkhu dwells in comfort.
Here, Anuruddha, a bhikkhunī hears:
“The bhikkhunī named so-and-so has passed away.”
The Blessed One has declared of her:
"She stands in final knowledge.
Furthermore, that sister has either seen it for herself or heard of it through tradition:
‘Such was her virtue,’ ‘such was her Dhamma,’ ‘such was her wisdom,’ ‘such was her way of abiding,’ ‘such was her liberation’—
recalling her faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, she directs her mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, a bhikkhunī dwells in comfort.
In this case, Anuruddha, a bhikkhunī hears:
“The bhikkhunī named so-and-so has passed away;
she was declared by the Blessed One—”
‘With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, she has become one of spontaneous birth, destined there for final Nibbāna, no longer subject to returning from that world.
Moreover, that sister was either personally seen by her [the nun] or heard of through tradition:
‘That sister had such virtue,’ and so on; ‘that sister had such Dhamma... such wisdom... such a mode of dwelling... such liberation.’”
Recalling her faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, she directs her mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, a bhikkhunī dwells in comfort.
Here, Anuruddha, a bhikkhunī hears:
‘The bhikkhunī named so-and-so has passed away;
she was declared by the Blessed One:

“With the total destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, she is a once-returner who, having come back to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering.”’
Furthermore, that sister has either seen her personally or heard of her by report:
“That sister was of such virtue, such a nature, ... [as above] ... such wisdom, such a mode of dwelling, and such liberation.
Recalling her faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, she directs her mind toward that same goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, there is a comfortable dwelling for a bhikkhunī.
Here, Anuruddha, a bhikkhunī hears:
“The bhikkhunī named so-and-so has passed away.”
She was declared by the Blessed One:
"With the complete destruction of the three fetters, she is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.
Furthermore, that sister had either seen it for herself or heard it through tradition:
‘Such was her virtue,’ ‘such was her Dhamma,’ ‘such was her wisdom,’ ‘such was her way of abiding,’ ‘such was her liberation’—
recalling her faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, she directs her mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, a bhikkhunī dwells in comfort.
In this case, Anuruddha, a lay follower hears:
"The lay follower named so-and-so has passed away;
he was declared by the Blessed One—"
‘With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to return from that world.
Moreover, that venerable one has been seen by him personally, or he has heard of him through oral tradition:
‘Such was the virtue of that venerable one; such was his Dhamma; such was his wisdom; such was his mode of living; such was his liberation.’”
Thus, recollecting his faith, learning, generosity, and wisdom, he directs his mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddhas, there is a comfortable dwelling for a lay follower.
Here, Anuruddhas, a lay follower hears:
‘The lay follower named so-and-so has passed away;
he was declared by the Blessed One:

“With the total destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is a once-returner who, having come back to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering.”’
Furthermore, that venerable one has either seen for himself or heard by tradition concerning him:
"Such was the virtue of that venerable one; such was his Dhamma... such was his wisdom... such was his way of abiding... such was his liberation, indeed.
Recalling his faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, he directs his mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddhas, there is a comfortable dwelling for a lay follower.
Here, Anuruddhas, a lay follower hears:
"A certain lay follower has passed away; [he was one who had such-and-such virtues]."
"He has been declared by the Blessed One:
'With the complete destruction of the three fetters, he is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.
Furthermore, that venerable one is either personally seen by him or heard of through tradition."
‘Such was the virtue of that venerable one,’ and ‘such was his Dhamma... such was his wisdom... such was his mode of dwelling...
such was his liberation,’ he directs his mind toward that goal, recollecting his faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
In this way too, Anuruddhas, there is a comfortable dwelling for a lay follower.
In this case, Anuruddha, a female lay follower hears:
"The female lay follower named so-and-so has passed away;
she was declared by the Blessed One—"
‘With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, she has been spontaneously reborn there and will attain final Nibbāna from that world, being no longer subject to return.
Furthermore, that sister was either personally seen by you or heard of through tradition:
‘That sister had such virtue,’ and so on, ‘that sister had such a nature... such wisdom... such a mode of dwelling... such a liberation.’”
Recalling her faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, she directs her mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddha, a female lay follower dwells in comfort.
Here, Anuruddha, a female lay follower hears:
‘The female lay follower named so-and-so has passed away;
she was declared by the Blessed One:

“With the total destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, she is a once-returner who, having come back to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering.”’
Furthermore, that sister has either seen her personally or heard of her through hearsay:
"That sister was of such virtue, such Dhamma, such wisdom, such a mode of dwelling, and such liberation.
Recalling her faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, she directs her mind toward that same goal.
In this way too, Anuruddhas, there is a comfortable dwelling for a female lay follower.
Here, Anuruddhas, a female lay follower hears:
"A certain female lay follower has passed away;..."
The Blessed One has declared of her:
"With the complete destruction of the three fetters, she is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.
Furthermore, that sister has either seen this for herself or has heard it through tradition:
‘Such was her virtue,’ ‘such was her Dhamma,’ ‘such was her wisdom,’ ‘such was her mode of dwelling,’ ‘such was her liberation’—
recalling her faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, she directs her mind toward that goal.
In this way too, Anuruddhas, a female lay follower dwells in comfort.

Thus, Anuruddha, the Tathāgata does not declare the rebirths of disciples who have passed away and died—saying, “So-and-so has been reborn there; so-and-so has been reborn there”—for the sake of deceiving people, nor for the sake of flattering people, nor for the sake of gain, honor, and renown, nor with the thought, “Let the world know me thus.
However, Anuruddha, there are sons of noble family who possess faith, sublime inspiration, and sublime joy.
Having heard this, they apply their minds toward that goal.
For them, Anuruddha, this leads to welfare and happiness for a long time.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Anuruddha, gladdened, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Naḷakapāna Sutta, the eighth, is concluded.
